description_full: Methanex Corporation engages in the production and sale of methanol and ammonia in Asia Pacific, North America, Europe, and South America. It also owns and leases in-region storage and terminal facilities. The company serves chemical and petrochemical producers. Methanex Corporation was incorporated in 1968 and is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada.
ceo_bio: Mr. Richard W. Sumner | President, CEO & Director | Age 50 | Compensation: $2.4M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $2.2M ranks in the top quartile among Basic Materials peers. Each employee generates $556K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: Methanex Corporation is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $5.5B market cap on $3.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -6% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $917M in free cash flow — roughly 26 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 7.01× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 7.4% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Piotroski score 3/9 — the fundamentals are deteriorating on multiple fronts
Altman Z in the distress zone (1.8) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Trading near 52-week highs — the market has already recognised the story (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Valued at a 34% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
23 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 12% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.92x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 70% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 50% and a beta of 0.81, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.82 vs 5y 0.71), so read it loosely.
About $39.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 76% in the 2020 crash, 48% in the 2022 bear market and 81% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $55.26 (margin of safety -28%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $35.69 to $83.96 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: EV/EBITDA 5.5 vs 8.3 and P/FCF 6.0 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 61% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 16.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $78.60 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 8.3%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.71).
It converts 26% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 6% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.0x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.6x net debt to EBITDA ($425.3M of cash against $2.7B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.0x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.81 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -5.9% over 3 years and 6.3% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 27%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 22.5% a year over five years.
It has missed earnings estimates by 31.1% on average.
Analysts expect -37.1% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 7.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 89%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.0% (1.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 23 consecutive years, raising it 8.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 1,649 employees, each generates about $2.2M of revenue, 3.5x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 2.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $556K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (1x revenue per employee).
